indicators.title: GDP per Person Employed
indicators.subtitle: India, 1991-2025
indicators.details:
What it shows — Output per worker in constant 2021 PPP dollars, a standard measure of labour productivity. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 24,842.11 PPP $ per worker in 2025. A rising line means each worker produces more; the gap to peers shows the productivity deficit.

Why it matters — Productivity growth is the only sustainable route to higher wages.

series.note: GDP per Person Employed: India's annual series, 1991 to 2025; the latest value is 24,842.11 PPP $ per worker. Source: World Bank API SL.GDP.PCAP.EM.KD (World Bank national accounts / ILO); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: GDP per Person Employed: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours
indicators.details:
What it shows — Output per worker in constant 2021 PPP dollars, a standard measure of labour productivity. This chart overlays India with 6 comparison countries.

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. A rising line means each worker produces more; the gap to peers shows the productivity deficit.

Why it matters — Productivity growth is the only sustainable route to higher wages.

series.note: GDP per Person Employed: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API SL.GDP.PCAP.EM.KD (World Bank national accounts / ILO); latest year with data: 2025.

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2025; India ranks 12 of 15 (1 = highest value). A rising line means each worker produces more; the gap to peers shows the productivity deficit.

Why it matters — Productivity growth is the only sustainable route to higher wages.

datasets.label: GDP per Person Employed: Peer Ranking (2025)

indicators.title: Manufacturing Value Added
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2025
indicators.details:
What it shows — Value added by manufacturing in current US dollars, the output created by factories net of inputs. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 532.92 USD bn in 2025. Bigger bars or slices mean larger factory output in dollar terms.

Why it matters — Manufacturing scale shows India's weight in global industry.

series.note: Manufacturing Value Added: India's annual series, 1980 to 2025; the latest value is 532.92 USD bn. Source: World Bank API NV.IND.MANF.CD (World Bank national accounts / ILO); latest year with data: 2025.

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2025; India ranks 3 of 13 (1 = highest value). Bigger bars or slices mean larger factory output in dollar terms.

Why it matters — Manufacturing scale shows India's weight in global industry.

series.note: Manufacturing Value Added, 2025: India ranks 3 of 13 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API NV.IND.MANF.CD (World Bank national accounts / ILO); latest year with data: 2025.

Why it matters — Manufacturing scale shows India's weight in global industry.

indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2025
indicators.details:

How to read it — The line ends at 445.28 USD bn in 2025. Higher bars show larger goods-trading nations; India's slice shows its share of the group's exports.

Why it matters — Goods exports reflect industrial competitiveness and supply-chain integration.

series.note: Merchandise Exports: India's annual series, 1980 to 2025; the latest value is 445.28 USD bn. Source: World Bank API TX.VAL.MRCH.CD.WT (World Bank / WTO / UNCTAD trade statistics); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Merchandise Trade Balance
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2025
indicators.details:
What it shows — Merchandise exports minus merchandise imports, in US dollars. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at -308.2 USD bn in 2025. Negative values are trade deficits; positive are surpluses.

Why it matters — India's chronic goods deficit shapes the current account and the rupee.

series.note: Merchandise Trade Balance: India's annual series, 1980 to 2025; the latest value is -308.2 USD bn. Source: World Bank API TX.VAL.MRCH.CD.WT, TM.VAL.MRCH.CD.WT (World Bank / WTO / UNCTAD trade statistics); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Export Volume Index (2015 = 100)
indicators.subtitle: India, 2005-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Quantity of goods exported, stripped of price effects, with 2015 set to 100. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 138.1 index in 2024. A steeper rise means the physical volume of exports is growing faster.

Why it matters — Volume shows real export capacity independent of commodity-price swings.

series.note: Export Volume Index (2015 = 100): India's annual series, 2005 to 2024; the latest value is 138.1 index. Source: World Bank API TX.QTY.MRCH.XD.WD (World Bank / WTO / UNCTAD trade statistics); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Net Barter Terms of Trade (2015 = 100)
indicators.subtitle: India, 2005-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Export prices relative to import prices; higher means each unit of exports buys more imports. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 91.3 index in 2024. A falling line means imports are getting dearer relative to exports.

Why it matters — Terms of trade drive real income gains and losses from trade.

series.note: Net Barter Terms of Trade (2015 = 100): India's annual series, 2005 to 2024; the latest value is 91.3 index. Source: World Bank API TT.PRI.MRCH.XD.WD (World Bank / WTO / UNCTAD trade statistics); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.subtitle: India, 1990-2022
indicators.details:

How to read it — The line ends at 4.59% in 2022. Lower values mean freer trade; bars show how protected each economy is.

Why it matters — Tariff levels shape the cost of inputs and India's access to global value chains.

series.note: Applied Tariff Rate: India's annual series, 1990 to 2022; the latest value is 4.59%. Source: World Bank API TM.TAX.MRCH.WM.AR.ZS (World Bank / WTO / UNCTAD trade statistics); latest year with data: 2022.

series.note: Applied Tariff Rate, 2022: India ranks 6 of 13 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API TM.TAX.MRCH.WM.AR.ZS (World Bank / WTO / UNCTAD trade statistics); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Logistics Performance Index
indicators.subtitle: India, 2007-2022
indicators.details:
What it shows — World Bank survey score (1 to 5) covering customs, infrastructure, shipments, tracking and timeliness. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 3.4 score in 2022. A higher score means smoother and cheaper movement of goods.

Why it matters — Logistics efficiency is a major hidden cost in Indian manufacturing.

series.note: Logistics Performance Index: India's annual series, 2007 to 2022; the latest value is 3.4 score. Source: World Bank API LP.LPI.OVRL.XQ (World Bank / WTO / UNCTAD trade statistics); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Iron ore production
indicators.subtitle: National iron ore mining output
indicators.details:
Iron ore is the primary raw material for steelmaking and industrial infrastructure. India is among the world's largest iron ore producers, led by Odisha, Chhattisgarh, and Karnataka.

Data is sourced from the Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) and Ministry of Mines.

series.source: Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) & Ministry of Mines (Iron Ore Production Output in Million Tonnes)

indicators.title: Bauxite production
indicators.subtitle: Bauxite ore mining output
indicators.details:
Bauxite is the principal ore for aluminium smelting, vital for aerospace, power transmission, automotive, and packaging industries.

Sourced from IBM and Ministry of Mines annual mineral reports.

series.source: IBM & Aluminium Association of India (Bauxite Production Output in Million Tonnes)

indicators.title: Refined copper production
indicators.subtitle: Refined copper metal production
indicators.details:
Refined copper is essential for electrical grids, electric vehicles, electronics, and urban infrastructure.

Data collated from Ministry of Mines and Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL).

series.source: Ministry of Mines & Hindustan Copper (Refined Copper Production Output in Thousand Tonnes)

indicators.title: Manganese ore output
indicators.subtitle: Manganese ore mining production
indicators.details:
Manganese ore is a crucial alloy element in steel manufacturing and battery technologies.

Sourced from Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) Annual Mineral Statistics.

series.source: Indian Bureau of Mines Annual Mineral Statistics (Manganese Ore Production Output in Lakh Tonnes)

indicators.title: Coal production trajectory
indicators.subtitle: Domestic coal mining output
indicators.details:
Coal is India's primary baseload energy source, fueling thermal power stations, steel plants, and heavy manufacturing.

Sourced from Coal Controller's Organisation and Ministry of Coal.

series.source: Coal Controller's Organisation & Ministry of Coal (Total Domestic Coal Production in Million Tonnes)

indicators.title: Lignite production
indicators.subtitle: Lignite mining output
indicators.details:
Lignite (brown coal) is mined predominantly in Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, and Gujarat for regional thermal power generation.

Sourced from NLC India Limited and Ministry of Coal.

series.source: NLC India & Ministry of Coal (Lignite Production Output in Million Tonnes)

indicators.title: Domestic crude oil production
indicators.subtitle: Domestic crude petroleum output
indicators.details:
Domestic crude oil production from onshore and offshore fields (Mumbai High, Assam, Rajasthan, KG Basin) supplies domestic refineries alongside energy imports.

Sourced from Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas (MoPNG) and PPAC.

series.source: Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas / PPAC (Domestic Crude Oil Production in Million Metric Tonnes)

indicators.title: Natural gas production
indicators.subtitle: Domestic natural gas production
indicators.details:
Natural gas is a clean energy transition fuel used in fertilizer production, city gas distribution (CGD), power plants, and industrial heating.

Sourced from Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) and MoPNG.

series.source: Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) & MoPNG (Domestic Natural Gas Production in Billion Cubic Metres - BCM)

indicators.title: Limestone production
indicators.subtitle: Limestone mining for cement & steel

indicators.title: Energy Intensity of GDP
indicators.subtitle: India, 1990-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Energy use per 1,000 dollars of GDP at PPP, a measure of how efficiently an economy uses energy. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 82.47 kg oil eq per $1,000 in 2024. A falling line means India squeezes more output from each unit of energy.

Why it matters — Lower energy intensity reduces import bills and emissions for every rupee of growth.

indicators.title: Women with a Financial Account
indicators.subtitle: India, 2011-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of adult women owning an account at a bank, other financial institution or mobile-money provider. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 89.25% of women 15+ in 2024. Points rise survey by survey; the gap to the 100% mark is the unbanked women's share.

Why it matters — Women's account ownership is the base on which digital credit and payments can scale.

series.note: Women with a Financial Account: India's annual series, 2011 to 2024; the latest value is 89.25% of women 15+. Source: World Bank API FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS (World Bank Global Findex / IMF); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Basic Drinking Water: Urban vs Rural India
indicators.subtitle: India, 2000-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of urban and rural populations using at least a basic drinking-water service.

How to read it — The distance between the lines is the rural deficit; converging lines mean the gap is closing.

Why it matters — Rural water access is central to the health gains targeted by regional programmes.

series.note: Basic Drinking Water: Urban vs Rural India, 2000 to 2024. Source: World Bank API SH.H2O.BASW.UR.ZS, SH.H2O.BASW.RU.ZS (WHO / UNICEF JMP / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Basic Sanitation: Urban vs Rural India
indicators.subtitle: India, 2000-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of urban and rural people using at least basic sanitation facilities.

How to read it — A steeper rural line means faster catch-up after the Swachh Bharat push.

Why it matters — Sanitation gaps drive diarrhoeal disease and child stunting in rural regions.

series.note: Basic Sanitation: Urban vs Rural India, 2000 to 2024. Source: World Bank API SH.STA.BASS.UR.ZS, SH.STA.BASS.RU.ZS (WHO / UNICEF JMP / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Electricity Access: Urban vs Rural India
indicators.subtitle: India, 1993-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of urban and rural populations with access to electricity.

How to read it — Both lines near 100% mean the divide has effectively closed.

Why it matters — Electrification is the precondition for rural clinics, schools and enterprises.

series.note: Electricity Access: Urban vs Rural India, 1993 to 2024. Source: World Bank API EG.ELC.ACCS.UR.ZS, EG.ELC.ACCS.RU.ZS (WHO / UNICEF JMP / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Open Defecation: Urban vs Rural India
indicators.subtitle: India, 2000-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of urban and rural people practising open defecation.

How to read it — Falling lines are progress; the rural line starts much higher.

Why it matters — Open defecation is a direct driver of infection and malnutrition.

series.note: Open Defecation: Urban vs Rural India, 2000 to 2024. Source: World Bank API SH.STA.ODFC.UR.ZS, SH.STA.ODFC.RU.ZS (WHO / UNICEF JMP / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Population: Urban vs Rural India
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2025
indicators.details:
What it shows — Absolute urban and rural population living in India.

How to read it — Where the lines cross shows when urban numbers overtake rural ones; rural numbers are flattening.

Why it matters — The balance of urban and rural people drives service demand across states.

series.note: Population: Urban vs Rural India, 1980 to 2025. Source: World Bank API SP.URB.TOTL, SP.RUR.TOTL (WHO / UNICEF JMP / World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Urban-Rural Gap in Basic Water Access: Peer Ranking (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Urban minus rural share of people with basic drinking water, in percentage points. Fifteen countries are ranked on the latest year with broad coverage.

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2024; India ranks 7 of 14 (1 = highest value). Bigger bars are bigger rural disadvantages; near zero means equal access.

Why it matters — The gap pinpoints where rural investment is still lagging.

datasets.label: Urban-Rural Gap in Basic Water Access: Peer Ranking (2024)

series.note: Urban-Rural Gap in Basic Water Access, 2024: India ranks 7 of 14 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API SH.H2O.BASW.UR.ZS, SH.H2O.BASW.RU.ZS (WHO / UNICEF JMP / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Urban-Rural Gap in Basic Sanitation: Peer Ranking (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Urban minus rural share of people with basic sanitation, in percentage points. Fifteen countries are ranked on the latest year with broad coverage.

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2024; India ranks 4 of 14 (1 = highest value). Larger positive bars show rural populations being left behind.

Why it matters — Closing this gap is a prerequisite for equal health outcomes across regions.

datasets.label: Urban-Rural Gap in Basic Sanitation: Peer Ranking (2024)

series.note: Urban-Rural Gap in Basic Sanitation, 2024: India ranks 4 of 14 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API SH.STA.BASS.UR.ZS, SH.STA.BASS.RU.ZS (WHO / UNICEF JMP / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Population in Largest City
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2025
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of the urban population living in the country's largest city. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 6.64% of urban population in 2025. Low values mean urban growth is spread over many cities rather than concentrated.

Why it matters — Dispersed urbanisation reduces pressure on a single megacity.

series.note: Population in Largest City: India's annual series, 1980 to 2025; the latest value is 6.64% of urban population. Source: World Bank API EN.URB.LCTY.UR.ZS (UN World Urbanization Prospects via World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

Why it matters — Dispersed urbanisation reduces pressure on a single megacity.

indicators.title: Population in Million-Plus Cities
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2025
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of the total population living in cities of more than one million people. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 16.96% of population in 2025. A rising line shows people migrating into large metros.

Why it matters — Large-city share influences housing, transport and health demand.

series.note: Population in Million-Plus Cities: India's annual series, 1980 to 2025; the latest value is 16.96% of population. Source: World Bank API EN.URB.MCTY.TL.ZS (UN World Urbanization Prospects via World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

Why it matters — Large-city share influences housing, transport and health demand.

indicators.title: Urban Population Growth: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours
indicators.details:
What it shows — Annual growth rate of the urban population. This chart overlays India with 6 comparison countries.

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. Higher bars mean faster-expanding cities.

Why it matters — Rapid urban growth tests housing and service delivery in city regions.

series.note: Urban Population Growth: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API SP.URB.GROW (UN World Urbanization Prospects via World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Urban Share of Population: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours
indicators.details:
What it shows — Urban population as a share of total population. This chart overlays India with 6 comparison countries.

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. Lines further up show more urbanised countries; India is still mostly rural.

Why it matters — Urban share is a core development benchmark.

series.note: Urban Share of Population: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API SP.URB.TOTL.IN.ZS (UN World Urbanization Prospects via World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Urban Population
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2025
indicators.details:
What it shows — Absolute number of people living in urban areas. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 522.44 million in 2025. The slice shows India's share of urban people across the 15 countries.

Why it matters — India adds some of the world's largest urban populations each year.

series.note: Urban Population: India's annual series, 1980 to 2025; the latest value is 522.44 million. Source: World Bank API SP.URB.TOTL (UN World Urbanization Prospects via World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Urban Population: Share Among Peers (2025)
indicators.subtitle: Each country's share of the 15-country total
indicators.details:
What it shows — Absolute number of people living in urban areas. Slices show each country's share of the sampled countries' total.

How to read it — Slices are shares of the group total in 2025; India holds 19.2% and ranks 2 of 15. A bigger slice means a larger absolute amount, not a better outcome.

Why it matters — India adds some of the world's largest urban populations each year.

series.note: Urban Population, 2025: India holds 19.2% of the group total and ranks 2 of 15. Source: World Bank API SP.URB.TOTL (UN World Urbanization Prospects via World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Rural Population Growth
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2025
indicators.details:
What it shows — Annual growth rate of the rural population. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 0.41% in 2025. A line crossing below zero means the rural population is shrinking.

Why it matters — Rural decline reflects migration to towns and falling fertility.

series.note: Rural Population Growth: India's annual series, 1980 to 2025; the latest value is 0.41%. Source: World Bank API SP.RUR.TOTL.ZG (UN World Urbanization Prospects via World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

How to read it — Lower is better. It is a three-year average, so it moves slowly.

Why it matters — Hunger is SDG 2 and the target of the National Food Security Act and PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana; this is also an input to the Global Hunger Index.

series.note: Share of population below minimum calorie needs, %. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Child Stunting (modelled)
indicators.subtitle: Children under 5 too short for their age, %
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of children under five who are too short for their age, a sign of chronic undernutrition.

How to read it — Lower is better; the trend comes from UNICEF/WHO/World Bank modelled estimates that smooth survey years (NFHS).

Why it matters — Stunting harms brain development and lifetime earnings and is the main target of POSHAN Abhiyaan.

series.note: Children under 5 too short for their age, %. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator SH.STA.STNT.ZS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Measles Immunisation
indicators.subtitle: Children aged 12-23 months vaccinated, %
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of young children who have received the measles vaccine.

How to read it — Higher is better; at least 95% is needed to stop measles outbreaks. Dips show disruptions such as COVID-19.

Why it matters — Measles coverage is a bellwether for the whole routine-immunisation system under Mission Indradhanush.

series.note: Children aged 12-23 months vaccinated, %. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator SH.IMM.MEAS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Infant Mortality Rate by Sex (SRS)
indicators.subtitle: Deaths before age one per 1,000 live births
indicators.details:
What it shows — Out of every 1,000 babies born alive, how many die before their first birthday, from the Registrar General's Sample Registration System.

How to read it — All lines falling means more infants survive. Girls' mortality was once higher than boys', which is unusual biologically; watch whether that gap has closed.

Why it matters — Infant mortality is a summary of maternal health, nutrition, immunisation and sanitation; SDG 3 asks India to keep pushing it down.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 15 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Under-Five Mortality Rate by Sex (SRS)
indicators.subtitle: Deaths before age five per 1,000 live births
indicators.details:
What it shows — Deaths of children before their fifth birthday per 1,000 live births, from the Sample Registration System.

How to read it — Lower is better; the SDG target is 25 or fewer by 2030. Compare girls with boys for signs of gender bias in child care.

Why it matters — Under-five deaths are mostly preventable (pneumonia, diarrhoea, newborn complications), so this measures how well basic health services reach children.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 17 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Life Expectancy at Birth by Sex (SRS)
indicators.subtitle: Years, five-year moving periods
indicators.details:
What it shows — How many years a newborn would live on average if current death rates held, from SRS abridged life tables for overlapping five-year periods.

How to read it — Both lines rising means longer lives. Women overtook men in the 1990s and the gap has widened, the normal pattern as health care improves.

Why it matters — Life expectancy sums up a country's health in one number and shapes pension, health and elder-care planning.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 18 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Projected periods (2021-25 onward) published alongside the estimates are excluded.

indicators.title: Maternal Mortality Ratio (SRS)
indicators.subtitle: Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births
indicators.details:
What it shows — Women who die from pregnancy or childbirth complications per 100,000 live births, from SRS special bulletins on maternal mortality.

How to read it — Each bar is a pooled period (for example 2018-20). India has passed its National Health Policy target of 100 and is heading toward the SDG goal of 70.

Why it matters — The fall reflects institutional deliveries under Janani Suraksha Yojana and better emergency obstetric care, and shows what is left to do.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 21 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Maternal Mortality Ratio by State (SRS) (2021-23)
indicators.subtitle: Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births
indicators.details:
What it shows — The maternal mortality ratio in each larger State for the latest SRS period.

How to read it — Longer bars are worse. Assam, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh usually rank highest; Kerala, Maharashtra and Telangana lowest.

Why it matters — The spread between States shows that national progress hides large regional gaps where maternal-health spending is most needed.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 21 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2021-23. Ranked highest to lowest.

indicators.title: Malaria Cases (NCVBDC)
indicators.subtitle: Reported cases nationwide
indicators.details:
What it shows — Malaria cases reported through the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control, with the more dangerous P. falciparum cases shown separately.

How to read it — Falling lines mean fewer infections; India's caseload has dropped by more than 80% since 2015.

Why it matters — India aims to eliminate malaria by 2030, so steady declines, especially in falciparum cases, track progress toward that goal.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 119 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Values for 2023, 2024 are marked provisional by the source. National totals are the sum of State/UT reports; the most recent years are provisional.

indicators.title: Dengue Cases (NCVBDC)
indicators.subtitle: Reported cases nationwide
indicators.details:
What it shows — Laboratory-reported dengue cases in India each year.

How to read it — Bars swing with monsoon conditions and urban mosquito breeding; the long-run trend is upward, partly because testing has improved.

Why it matters — Dengue is an expanding urban health threat linked to water storage, construction and a warming climate, with no widely used vaccine yet.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 120 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Values for 2023 are marked provisional by the source. National totals are the sum of State/UT reports; the most recent years are provisional.

indicators.title: Population
indicators.subtitle: Total population
indicators.details:
Population provides the denominator and demographic context for many other indicators. A growing population can expand the workforce and consumer base while also increasing demand for jobs, housing, health, and infrastructure.

This is a count of people, not a welfare measure. Per-capita indicators and age structure are needed to understand how demographic change affects living standards.

indicators.title: Unemployment rate
indicators.subtitle: Share of the labour force without work
indicators.details:
The unemployment rate measures the share of the labour force that is without work but available for and seeking employment. It does not capture underemployment or people who have stopped looking for work.

Labour-market comparisons require care because survey design and informal employment affect measurement. This annual series is a useful macro context signal rather than a complete employment dashboard.

indicators.title: Electricity access
indicators.subtitle: Population with access to electricity
indicators.details:
Electricity access measures the share of the population with access to electricity. It is a core infrastructure and living-conditions indicator with direct relevance to households, schools, businesses, and digital services.

Coverage does not fully describe reliability, affordability, or quality of supply. The series is annual and sourced through the open World Bank API.

indicators.title: Internet users
indicators.subtitle: Individuals using the internet
indicators.details:
Internet use measures the share of people using the internet. It provides a broad signal of digital access and the potential reach of online services, payments, education, and commerce.

The metric does not measure connection speed, affordability, quality, or intensity of use. Those dimensions require more detailed telecom and household datasets.

indicators.title: Life expectancy
indicators.subtitle: Life expectancy at birth
indicators.details:
Life expectancy at birth estimates the average years a newborn would live under current mortality conditions. It is a high-level outcome indicator for population health and social development.

It is not an individual prediction and does not reveal regional, gender, or income differences. Trends should be interpreted alongside health-system and demographic data.

indicators.title: Youth Unemployment (ILO estimate)
indicators.subtitle: Unemployed as % of labour force aged 15-24
indicators.details:
What it shows — The ILO-modelled unemployment rate for young people aged 15-24, comparable across countries.

How to read it — Read it with the PLFS youth chart: the methods differ, but both show youth unemployment far above the overall rate.

Why it matters — It shows how well the economy absorbs new entrants into the workforce each year.

indicators.title: Women in Parliament
indicators.subtitle: Share of Lok Sabha seats held by women, %
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of seats in the lower house of Parliament held by women.

How to read it — Steps in the line follow general elections. The Women's Reservation Act (2023) will reserve one-third of seats once it takes effect.

Why it matters — Representation shapes which issues reach the legislative agenda.

series.note: Share of Lok Sabha seats held by women, %. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator SG.GEN.PARL.ZS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Research & Development Spending
indicators.subtitle: Gross domestic spending on R&D, % of GDP
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total spending on research and development by government, business and universities as a share of GDP.

How to read it — India's figure stays near 0.7%, against about 2.5% in China and over 3% in the US and South Korea.

Why it matters — R&D drives innovation and productivity; the Anusandhan National Research Foundation is meant to lift private research spending.

series.note: Gross domestic spending on R&D, % of GDP. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator GB.XPD.RSDV.GD.ZS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Researchers per Million People
indicators.subtitle: Full-time researchers in R&D per million population
indicators.details:
What it shows — The number of people working full-time in research per million population.

How to read it — Higher means a larger research workforce; India's figure is low by international standards.

Why it matters — A country's research base decides its ability to innovate in fields from vaccines to semiconductors.

series.note: Full-time researchers in R&D per million population. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator SP.POP.SCIE.RD.P6); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Labour Force Participation Rate (PLFS)
indicators.subtitle: Share of people aged 15+ working or seeking work
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of people aged 15 and over who are in the labour force (working or looking for work), from the Periodic Labour Force Survey.

How to read it — Compare the women's line with the men's: the gap shows how many women are outside paid work. A rising women's line is the biggest labour-market change since 2017-18.

Why it matters — Participation, not just unemployment, decides how much of India's demographic dividend turns into output and household income.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Periodic Labour Force Survey, indicator 1 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Usual status (principal + subsidiary), rural + urban, agricultural years July-June.

indicators.title: Worker Population Ratio (PLFS)
indicators.subtitle: Share of people aged 15+ who are employed
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of the population aged 15 and over that is actually employed.

How to read it — This is the employment rate: it rises when jobs grow faster than population. Read it alongside the participation chart.

Why it matters — It is the most direct measure of how many people the economy employs, and it includes self-employment and unpaid family work.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Periodic Labour Force Survey, indicator 2 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Usual status (principal + subsidiary), rural + urban, agricultural years July-June.

indicators.title: Unemployment Rate (PLFS)
indicators.subtitle: Share of the labour force aged 15+ without work
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of people in the labour force (aged 15+) who looked for work but found none.

How to read it — Lower is better. A falling line together with a rising participation rate is a genuinely tightening labour market.

Why it matters — This is India's official headline unemployment measure, used for policy and to compare States.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Periodic Labour Force Survey, indicator 3 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Usual status (principal + subsidiary), rural + urban, agricultural years July-June.

indicators.title: Youth Unemployment Rate, 15-29 (PLFS)
indicators.subtitle: Share of the labour force aged 15-29 without work
indicators.details:
What it shows — The unemployment rate among young people aged 15-29.

How to read it — Youth unemployment runs well above the overall rate; watch the gap between young women and young men.

Why it matters — Joblessness among educated young people is a key political and economic issue and the target of skilling and apprenticeship schemes.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Periodic Labour Force Survey, indicator 3 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Usual status (principal + subsidiary), rural + urban, agricultural years July-June.

indicators.title: Sex Ratio at Birth (SRS)
indicators.subtitle: Girls born per 1,000 boys, three-year periods
indicators.details:
What it shows — How many girls are born for every 1,000 boys, from the Sample Registration System.

How to read it — The natural ratio is about 950. Values well below that point to sex-selective abortion; an upward trend means the gap is closing.

Why it matters — This is the key outcome for Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and the PC-PNDT Act, and it shapes future marriage markets and demography.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 7 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Population Sex Ratio (Census 1951-2011)
indicators.subtitle: Females per 1,000 males
indicators.details:
What it shows — Females per 1,000 males in the whole population at each Census from 1951 to 2011.

How to read it — A value below 1,000 means fewer women than men. India's ratio dipped to 927 in 1991 and recovered to 943 by 2011.

Why it matters — A persistently low sex ratio reflects excess female mortality and son preference; it is one of the starkest gender indicators.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 2 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Women's Mean Age at Marriage (SRS)
indicators.subtitle: Average age at effective marriage, years
indicators.details:
What it shows — The average age at which women marry, from the Sample Registration System.

How to read it — Higher is better for health and education outcomes. Urban women marry about two years later than rural women.

Why it matters — Later marriage is linked to more schooling, lower fertility and better maternal and child health; it is also behind the debate on raising the legal age of marriage to 21.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 14 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Total Fertility Rate by Women's Education (SRS) (2023)
indicators.subtitle: Children per woman
indicators.details:
What it shows — The average number of children a woman would have over her life, grouped by her education level, for the latest SRS year.

How to read it — Bars fall from left to right: illiterate women have the most children and graduates the fewest.

Why it matters — Girls' education is one of the most powerful levers on population growth, maternal health and child welfare.

datasets.label: Total Fertility Rate by Women's Education (SRS) (2023)

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 10 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2023.

indicators.title: Literacy Rate by Sex (age 7+)
indicators.subtitle: Census 1981-2011 and NSS 2017-18, %
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of people aged seven and over who can read and write, from the Census and the NSS 75th round (2017-18).

How to read it — The gap between men's and women's lines is the gender literacy gap; it has narrowed steadily since 1981.

Why it matters — Literacy is the base for employability, health awareness and civic participation, and women's literacy in particular predicts child health.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 55 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Gross Enrolment Ratio by Stage (UDISE+/AISHE)
indicators.subtitle: Enrolment as % of the official age group
indicators.details:
What it shows — Enrolment at each stage of education as a percentage of the population of the matching age group.

How to read it — Primary is near or above 100% (universal), but each later stage is lower: the drop between lines shows where children leave school.

Why it matters — The National Education Policy targets 100% GER up to secondary level and 50% in higher education by 2035.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 60 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: School Dropout Rate by Stage (UDISE+)
indicators.subtitle: Average annual dropout rate, %
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of students who leave school during the year at each stage, from UDISE+.

How to read it — Lower is better. Secondary-stage dropout is several times higher than primary, which is where most children are lost.

Why it matters — Dropout shows whether rising enrolment turns into completed schooling; secondary dropout is the main focus of Samagra Shiksha.

series.note: Source: MoSPI Women & Men in India, indicator 74 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Number of Universities (AISHE)
indicators.subtitle: Universities and university-level institutions
indicators.details:
What it shows — The number of universities in India in each All India Survey on Higher Education.

How to read it — Each bar is an academic year; steady growth means new central, State, private and deemed universities opening.

Why it matters — More institutions widen access, but the quality of what is taught matters as much as the count.

series.note: Source: Ministry of Education AISHE via MoSPI, indicator 1 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Number of Colleges (AISHE)
indicators.subtitle: Colleges affiliated to universities
indicators.details:
What it shows — The number of colleges in India in each AISHE round.

How to read it — Bars rising year on year show expansion; most new colleges are private and small.

Why it matters — Colleges teach the bulk of India's undergraduates, so their spread decides how many students can get a degree near home.

series.note: Source: Ministry of Education AISHE via MoSPI, indicator 2 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Higher Education Enrolment by Sex (AISHE)
indicators.subtitle: Estimated students enrolled
indicators.details:
What it shows — The estimated number of students enrolled in higher education, split by sex.

How to read it — Women's enrolment has nearly caught up with men's; where the lines cross, women outnumber men.

Why it matters — Higher-education enrolment builds the skilled workforce, and women's rising share is one of India's quieter social shifts.

series.note: Source: Ministry of Education AISHE via MoSPI, indicator 3 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Higher Education Enrolment by Level (AISHE) (2021-22)
indicators.subtitle: Share of students by programme level
indicators.details:
What it shows — How students in higher education are spread across programme levels in the latest AISHE round.

How to read it — Undergraduates are the overwhelming majority; Ph.D. students are a sliver, which is relevant to India's research capacity.

Why it matters — The mix shows whether the system mostly produces first degrees or advanced skills and research.

series.note: Source: Ministry of Education AISHE via MoSPI, indicator 3 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2021-22.

indicators.title: Higher Education GER by Social Group (AISHE)
indicators.subtitle: Gross enrolment ratio, age 18-23, %
indicators.details:
What it shows — Higher-education enrolment as a share of the 18-23 age group for all students, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

How to read it — The gap between the 'All' line and the SC and ST lines measures unequal access; narrowing gaps mean more inclusive growth.

Why it matters — GER is the headline access measure under NEP 2020 (target 50% by 2035), and group gaps guide scholarships and reservation policy.

series.note: Source: Ministry of Education AISHE via MoSPI, indicator 6 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Higher Education GER by State (AISHE) (2021-22)
indicators.subtitle: Gross enrolment ratio, age 18-23, %
indicators.details:
What it shows — The higher-education gross enrolment ratio in each State and UT for the latest AISHE round.

How to read it — Longer bars mean more young people in college. Southern States and some UTs lead; large northern and eastern States trail.

Why it matters — State gaps show where new colleges, scholarships and hostels would do the most to raise national enrolment.

labels: Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu
series.note: Source: Ministry of Education AISHE via MoSPI, indicator 6 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2021-22. Ranked highest to lowest.

indicators.title: CO2 Emissions per Person
indicators.subtitle: Tonnes of CO2 per capita, excluding land use
indicators.details:
What it shows — Carbon dioxide released per Indian each year from fossil fuels, cement and industry.

How to read it — A rising line means emissions are growing faster than population. India's figure is about a third of the world average and a sixth of the US level.

Why it matters — Per-person emissions frame India's climate-equity argument: total emissions are large, but each citizen's footprint is small.

series.note: Tonnes of CO2 per capita, excluding land use. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator EN.GHG.CO2.PC.CE.AR5); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Total Greenhouse Gas Emissions
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes of CO2-equivalent, excluding land use
indicators.details:
What it shows — All greenhouse gases India emits each year (CO2, methane, nitrous oxide and F-gases), converted to CO2-equivalent.

How to read it — The slope shows how fast emissions are growing; compare it with GDP growth to judge whether the economy is decarbonising.

Why it matters — India is now the world's third-largest emitter in total, which makes its 2070 net-zero pathway globally significant.

series.note: Million tonnes of CO2-equivalent, excluding land use. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator EN.GHG.ALL.MT.CE.AR5); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Protected Areas
indicators.subtitle: Terrestrial and marine protected areas, % of territory
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of India's land and territorial waters inside national parks, sanctuaries and other protected areas.

How to read it — Higher is more protected; the global 30x30 target asks countries to protect 30% by 2030.

Why it matters — Protected areas safeguard tigers, elephants and watersheds, but expanding them must be balanced against forest-dwellers' rights.

series.note: Terrestrial and marine protected areas, % of territory. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator ER.PTD.TOTL.ZS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Renewable Freshwater per Person
indicators.subtitle: Cubic metres of internal renewable water per person
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much renewable freshwater (rivers and groundwater recharge) India has per person.

How to read it — The total resource is roughly fixed, so the line falls as population grows. Below 1,700 m3 a country is 'water-stressed'; below 1,000 it is 'water-scarce'.

Why it matters — Falling water per person explains groundwater depletion, inter-State river disputes and the push for micro-irrigation and Jal Jeevan Mission.

series.note: Cubic metres of internal renewable water per person. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator ER.H2O.INTR.PC); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Population Density
indicators.subtitle: People per square kilometre of land
indicators.details:
What it shows — The average number of people living on each square kilometre of India's land.

How to read it — A steadily rising line; India is one of the most densely populated large countries.

Why it matters — Density raises pressure on land, forests, water and cities, and shapes disaster exposure.

series.note: People per square kilometre of land. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator EN.POP.DNST); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: All-India Mean Temperature by Season
indicators.subtitle: Area-weighted average temperature, °C (IMD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — The India Meteorological Department's all-India average air temperature for the whole year and for each season, from 2001.

How to read it — Each line is one season. A line that drifts upward over the years means that season is getting warmer; compare the annual line with the pre-monsoon line to see where heat is concentrated.

Why it matters — Rising temperatures drive heat stress, crop losses, power demand and water scarcity, so this is the baseline for every climate-adaptation discussion.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 1 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: All-India Annual Rainfall
indicators.subtitle: Sum of monthly all-India rainfall, mm (IMD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total rainfall received across India in each calendar year, built by adding the IMD's twelve monthly all-India averages.

How to read it — Taller bars are wetter years. Look for short bars: they usually line up with drought years and weak monsoons, such as 2002, 2009 and 2014-15.

Why it matters — Roughly half of India's farmland is rain-fed, so a poor rainfall year shows up quickly in farm output, rural incomes, food prices and reservoir levels.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 3 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Southwest Monsoon Rainfall (June-September)
indicators.subtitle: Sum of June-September all-India rainfall, mm (IMD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Rain delivered by the southwest monsoon, the four months from June to September, in each year.

How to read it — Compare each bar with the others: the monsoon normally brings about three-quarters of India's annual rain, so dips here explain most dry years in the annual chart.

Why it matters — Kharif sowing, groundwater recharge, hydropower and rural demand all depend on the monsoon; the RBI and the Finance Ministry track it closely for inflation and growth.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 3 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Cyclonic Storms over the North Indian Ocean
indicators.subtitle: Storms formed in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea per year (IMD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — The number of cyclonic storms that formed each year over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea, as recorded by the IMD.

How to read it — Each bar counts storms, not damage. Year-to-year swings are natural; look at decades together to judge whether storms are becoming more frequent.

Why it matters — Cyclones threaten a coastline that is home to millions of people. Better forecasting and evacuation have cut deaths sharply even when storm counts have not fallen.

datasets.label: Cyclonic Storms over the North Indian Ocean

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 89 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Heat Wave Days by State (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Average heat wave days in the summer season (IMD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — How many heat wave days each State recorded in the most recent summer season, as declared by the IMD.

How to read it — Longer bars mean more days of dangerous heat. Northern and central plains usually top the list.

Why it matters — Heat waves kill outdoor workers, the elderly and the poor, cut labour productivity and stress power grids; State heat-action plans target the worst-hit regions.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 87 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2024. Ranked highest to lowest.

indicators.title: India's Forest Cover
indicators.subtitle: Total forest cover, sq km (Forest Survey of India)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total area under forest cover in India from each State of Forest Report, built from satellite mapping by the Forest Survey of India.

How to read it — Each point is one biennial assessment; a rising line means more mapped forest cover. Mapping methods and resolution have improved over time, so small changes are within error.

Why it matters — Forests store carbon, protect watersheds and support tribal livelihoods; India's climate pledge includes adding a carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes through forests and tree cover.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 20 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). The source files the national total under a State label in some years; it is detected and used as the all-India value.

indicators.title: Forest Cover by State (2023)
indicators.subtitle: Forest cover in the latest State of Forest Report, sq km
indicators.details:
What it shows — The forest area of each State and UT in the most recent State of Forest Report.

How to read it — Bars are absolute areas, so large States lead. Madhya Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Odisha usually hold the biggest forests.

Why it matters — Forest-rich States carry much of India's carbon sink and biodiversity; forest area is also one factor in how the Finance Commission shares central taxes with States.

labels: Daman and Diu and Dadra Nagar Haveli
series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 20 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2023. Ranked highest to lowest.

indicators.title: Municipal Solid Waste Generated by State (2021-22)
indicators.subtitle: Tonnes per day (CPCB)
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much municipal solid waste (household and commercial garbage) each State's urban local bodies generate per day, as reported to the Central Pollution Control Board.

How to read it — Longer bars mean more waste each day. Populous, urbanised States such as Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Delhi generate the most.

Why it matters — Waste volumes set the scale of collection, processing and landfill capacity cities need under the Solid Waste Management Rules and Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban).

datasets.label: Municipal Solid Waste Generated by State (2021-22)

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 80 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2021-22. Ranked highest to lowest. Values are shown as published; Uttarakhand's reported figure is unusually high relative to its population.

indicators.title: Urban Waste: Generated, Collected, Treated, Landfilled (2021-22)
indicators.subtitle: All-India municipal solid waste, tonnes per day (CPCB)
indicators.details:
What it shows — All-India totals of municipal solid waste generated, collected, scientifically treated and sent to landfill each day.

How to read it — Read the bars left to right as a funnel: the gap between Generated and Collected is waste left on streets, and the gap between Collected and Treated is waste dumped without processing.

Why it matters — The treated share is the clearest measure of whether cities are actually managing waste rather than just moving it to dumpsites.

datasets.label: Urban Waste: Generated, Collected, Treated, Landfilled (2021-22)

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 80 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2021-22. All-India figures are the sum of State/UT reports for the latest year.

indicators.title: Plastic Waste Generated
indicators.subtitle: Estimated plastic waste, tonnes per annum (CPCB)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Estimated plastic waste generated across India each year, summed from State Pollution Control Board reports to the CPCB.

How to read it — Bars show the national total. Jumps can reflect better reporting by States as well as real growth in plastic use.

Why it matters — Plastic waste clogs drains, pollutes rivers and seas and is the target of India's single-use plastic ban and Extended Producer Responsibility rules.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 132 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). National totals are the sum of State/UT estimates.

indicators.title: Deaths from Forces of Nature by Cause (2022)
indicators.subtitle: Share of accidental deaths due to natural causes (NCRB)
indicators.details:
What it shows — How deaths attributed to forces of nature in the latest year split by cause, from NCRB's Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India.

How to read it — Bigger slices are bigger killers. Lightning is usually the largest single cause, ahead of floods and heat stroke.

Why it matters — Lightning and heat kill more people than dramatic disasters such as earthquakes, which points disaster-risk spending toward early warnings and shelters.

datasets.label: Deaths from Forces of Nature by Cause (2022)

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 94 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2022.

indicators.title: Deaths from Forces of Nature
indicators.subtitle: Total accidental deaths due to natural causes (NCRB)
indicators.details:
What it shows — The total number of people killed by natural causes (lightning, floods, heat, cold, landslides, storms and others) each year.

How to read it — Each bar is one year. Spikes usually match a severe flood, cyclone or heat season.

Why it matters — This tracks the human cost of climate and weather extremes, and whether early-warning systems are saving lives.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 94 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Electricity Generation by Source (2023-24)
indicators.subtitle: Share of gross generation, GWh (CEA)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Where India's electricity came from in the latest year, by fuel, from Central Electricity Authority data.

How to read it — Each slice is a share of total generation. Coal still dominates; the renewables slice (solar, wind, small hydro, biomass) is the one to watch.

Why it matters — India has pledged 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070, so the coal-to-renewables balance is the core energy-transition metric.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 41 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2023-24.

indicators.title: Electricity Generation since Independence
indicators.subtitle: Gross generation by source, GWh (CEA)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Gross electricity generated in India by source from 1947 to the latest year.

How to read it — Lines show absolute output, so thermal power's steep climb shows how India electrified. Renewables appear only from the 2000s and are now rising fastest.

Why it matters — Electricity use tracks industrialisation and living standards; the mix shows how carbon-intensive that growth has been.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 41 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

How to read it — The line ends at 3,153.8 Mt CO2e in 2024. Bigger bars or slices are bigger absolute emitters.

Why it matters — India's rank shows its weight in global climate outcomes.

series.note: CO2 Emissions: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 3,153.8 Mt CO2e. Source: World Bank API EN.GHG.CO2.MT.CE.AR5 (EDGAR / CAIT / World Bank climate data); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Methane Emissions
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Methane emissions, mostly from agriculture, livestock and waste, in CO2 equivalent. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 861.61 Mt CO2e in 2024. Rising lines show growth in livestock and rice farming.

Why it matters — Methane is a potent short-lived warming gas where quick cuts pay off.

series.note: Methane Emissions: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 861.61 Mt CO2e. Source: World Bank API EN.GHG.CH4.MT.CE.AR5 (EDGAR / CAIT / World Bank climate data); latest year with data: 2024.

Why it matters — Methane is a potent short-lived warming gas where quick cuts pay off.

series.note: Methane Emissions, 2024: India ranks 2 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API EN.GHG.CH4.MT.CE.AR5 (EDGAR / CAIT / World Bank climate data); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Carbon Intensity of GDP
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Kilograms of CO2 emitted per dollar of GDP in constant prices. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 0.92 kg CO2 per $ GDP in 2024. A falling line means growth is decoupling from emissions.

Why it matters — Intensity is the metric behind India's climate pledge.

series.note: Carbon Intensity of GDP: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 0.92 kg CO2 per $ GDP. Source: World Bank API EN.GHG.CO2.RT.GDP.KD (EDGAR / CAIT / World Bank climate data); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours
indicators.details:

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. A falling line means growth is decoupling from emissions.

Why it matters — Intensity is the metric behind India's climate pledge.

series.note: Carbon Intensity of GDP: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API EN.GHG.CO2.RT.GDP.KD (EDGAR / CAIT / World Bank climate data); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Total GHG Emissions per Capita
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — All greenhouse gases per person in tonnes of CO2 equivalent. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 3.01 t CO2e in 2024. India sits far below the lines for the US and China.

Why it matters — Per-capita emissions anchor the equity argument in climate diplomacy.

series.note: Total GHG Emissions per Capita: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 3.01 t CO2e. Source: World Bank API EN.GHG.ALL.PC.CE.AR5 (EDGAR / CAIT / World Bank climate data); latest year with data: 2024.

Why it matters — Per-capita emissions anchor the equity argument in climate diplomacy.

series.note: Total GHG Emissions per Capita: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API EN.GHG.ALL.PC.CE.AR5 (EDGAR / CAIT / World Bank climate data); latest year with data: 2024.

How to read it — The line ends at 100% of population in 2017. Near 100% means essentially all residents breathe unsafe air.

Why it matters — Exposure share frames air pollution as a nationwide issue.

Why it matters — India is among the largest water users globally.

indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2022

What it shows — Constant GDP produced per cubic metre of freshwater withdrawn. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 4.62 GDP $ per m3 in 2022. A rising line means more output per drop of water.

Why it matters — Water productivity measures efficiency gains in a water-scarce country.

series.note: Water Productivity: India's annual series, 1980 to 2022; the latest value is 4.62 GDP $ per m3. Source: World Bank API ER.GDP.FWTL.M3.KD (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. A rising line means more output per drop of water.

Why it matters — Water productivity measures efficiency gains in a water-scarce country.

series.note: Water Productivity: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API ER.GDP.FWTL.M3.KD (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

How to read it — Agriculture dominates the slice, so irrigation efficiency matters most. In 2022, Agriculture is the largest slice at 90.4%.

Why it matters — Sector shares show where water-saving policy would have the biggest effect.

series.note: India: Freshwater Withdrawals by Sector, 2022: Agriculture is the largest slice at 90.4%. Source: World Bank API ER.H2O.FWAG.ZS, ER.H2O.FWIN.ZS, ER.H2O.FWDM.ZS (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Average Annual Precipitation
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2022
indicators.details:
What it shows — Long-term average rainfall depth across the country. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 1,083 mm in 2022. India's rainfall is mostly monsoon-borne.

Why it matters — Rainfall underpins water supply and agricultural output.

series.note: Average Annual Precipitation: India's annual series, 1980 to 2022; the latest value is 1,083 mm. Source: World Bank API AG.LND.PRCP.MM (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Average Annual Precipitation: Peer Ranking (2022)
indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2022
indicators.details:
What it shows — Long-term average rainfall depth across the country. Fifteen countries are ranked on the latest year with broad coverage.

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2022; India ranks 8 of 15 (1 = highest value). India's rainfall is mostly monsoon-borne.

Why it matters — Rainfall underpins water supply and agricultural output.

series.note: Average Annual Precipitation, 2022: India ranks 8 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API AG.LND.PRCP.MM (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Fertiliser Use per Hectare
indicators.subtitle: Kg of N+P+K nutrients per hectare of arable land
indicators.details:
What it shows — How intensively Indian farmland is fertilised: kilograms of nitrogen, phosphate and potash applied per hectare.

How to read it — A rising line means more intensive farming. Compare it with cereal yields to see whether extra fertiliser still raises output.

Why it matters — Heavy, unbalanced fertiliser use raises the subsidy bill and degrades soil and groundwater, which is why soil-health cards and nano-urea are being promoted.

series.note: Kg of N+P+K nutrients per hectare of arable land. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator AG.CON.FERT.ZS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Irrigated Agricultural Land
indicators.subtitle: Share of agricultural land that is irrigated, %
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of India's agricultural land that receives irrigation rather than depending only on rain.

How to read it — Higher means farming is better protected from monsoon failures.

Why it matters — Irrigation is the biggest buffer against drought; PM Krishi Sinchayee Yojana aims to extend it to every farm.

series.note: Share of agricultural land that is irrigated, %. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator AG.LND.IRIG.AG.ZS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Arable Land per Person
indicators.subtitle: Hectares of arable land per person
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much cropland India has for each person.

How to read it — The line falls as population grows on a fixed land base; fragmentation means the average farm holding is now about one hectare.

Why it matters — Shrinking land per person makes productivity growth, not area expansion, the only route to feeding more people.

series.note: Hectares of arable land per person. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator AG.LND.ARBL.HA.PC); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Food Production Index
indicators.subtitle: Index of food output, 2014-2016 = 100
indicators.details:
What it shows — A volume index of all food crops and livestock produced in India, set to 100 for 2014-2016.

How to read it — A value of 120 means 20% more food than the 2014-16 average. Steady growth with few dips shows resilient farm output.

Why it matters — It summarises whether food supply is keeping pace with population and demand.

series.note: Index of food output, 2014-2016 = 100. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator AG.PRD.FOOD.XD); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Foodgrain Production
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes (Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare)
indicators.details:
What it shows — India's production of rice, wheat, coarse cereals (millets, maize) and pulses, and their total, for each crop year (July-June).

How to read it — The top line is total foodgrains; the lines below show what it is made of. Dips usually follow drought years such as 2009-10 and 2014-15.

Why it matters — Foodgrain output underpins food security, the public distribution system (PDS) and food inflation. Pulses matter because India still imports to meet demand.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 51 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Oilseed Production
indicators.subtitle: Lakh tonnes (Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Production of India's nine major oilseeds and the three biggest of them: soybean, rapeseed-mustard and groundnut.

How to read it — Compare the total with the three crops below it to see which crop is driving growth or decline.

Why it matters — India imports more than half of its edible oil, so domestic oilseed output decides the import bill and is the target of the National Mission on Edible Oils.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 51 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). The API labels these rows 'Million tonnes', but the magnitudes match the Ministry's lakh-tonne series (for example 2023-24 nine oilseeds = 416.7 lakh tonnes).

indicators.title: Sugarcane Production
indicators.subtitle: Lakh tonnes (Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total sugarcane harvested in India in each crop year.

How to read it — Higher values mean a bigger cane crop; the swings follow monsoon rainfall and irrigation in Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka.

Why it matters — Sugarcane feeds the sugar industry and the ethanol-blending programme, but it is very water-intensive, which ties it to groundwater depletion debates.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 51 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). The API labels these rows 'Million tonnes', but the magnitudes match the Ministry's lakh-tonne series (2023-24 = 4,351 lakh tonnes, about 435 million tonnes).

indicators.title: Fertiliser Consumption by Nutrient
indicators.subtitle: Lakh tonnes of N, P and K (Department of Fertilizers)
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much nitrogen, phosphate and potash fertiliser Indian farmers used each year since 1981-82, in nutrient terms.

How to read it — Nitrogen (mostly urea) towers over the others. The agronomic ideal is roughly 4:2:1 for N:P:K, so a widening gap signals unbalanced use.

Why it matters — Fertiliser subsidies are one of the largest items in the Union Budget, and overuse of urea degrades soil and water; this chart shows the scale of both.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 54 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Fertiliser: Consumption vs Production vs Imports
indicators.subtitle: Total N+P+K, lakh tonnes (Department of Fertilizers)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total fertiliser nutrients consumed in India against what was produced domestically and what was imported.

How to read it — When the consumption line sits above production, the gap is filled by imports. Watch whether new urea plants narrow that gap.

Why it matters — Import dependence exposes farmers and the subsidy bill to global gas and fertiliser prices, as in 2022.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 54 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Livestock Population by Species
indicators.subtitle: Million animals, Livestock Census (DAHD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — The number of cattle, buffaloes, goats, sheep and pigs counted in each Livestock Census since 1951.

How to read it — Each point is a census year. Cattle numbers have plateaued while buffaloes and goats have grown, reflecting the shift to dairy and meat.

Why it matters — Livestock supports about a fifth of rural households and makes India the world's largest milk producer.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 61 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Fish Production: Inland vs Marine
indicators.subtitle: Lakh tonnes (Department of Fisheries)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Fish produced in India each year from inland waters (rivers, reservoirs and fish farms) and from the sea.

How to read it — Inland production overtook marine catch in the 1990s and now dominates; that is the aquaculture boom.

Why it matters — India is the world's second-largest fish producer, and fisheries support millions of coastal and rural livelihoods and a major seafood-export trade.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 64 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Cereal Production
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total harvested production of wheat, rice, maize and other cereals. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 391.12 million tonnes in 2024. Bigger bars or slices are larger producers.

Why it matters — Cereals are the backbone of India's food supply.

series.note: Cereal Production: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 391.12 million tonnes. Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CREL.MT (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total harvested production of wheat, rice, maize and other cereals. Fifteen countries are ranked on the latest year with broad coverage.

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2024; India ranks 3 of 15 (1 = highest value). Bigger bars or slices are larger producers.

Why it matters — Cereals are the backbone of India's food supply.

series.note: Cereal Production, 2024: India ranks 3 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CREL.MT (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Cereal Production: Share Among Peers (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Each country's share of the 15-country total
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total harvested production of wheat, rice, maize and other cereals. Slices show each country's share of the sampled countries' total.

How to read it — Slices are shares of the group total in 2024; India holds 18.6% and ranks 3 of 15. A bigger slice means a larger absolute amount, not a better outcome.

Why it matters — Cereals are the backbone of India's food supply.

series.note: Cereal Production, 2024: India holds 18.6% of the group total and ranks 3 of 15. Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CREL.MT (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:

How to read it — The line ends at 129.64 index in 2024. A rising line means crop output is growing faster.

Why it matters — The index tracks output growth beyond land expansion.

series.note: Crop Production Index (2014-16 = 100): India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 129.64 index. Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CROP.XD (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

Why it matters — The index tracks output growth beyond land expansion.

series.note: Crop Production Index (2014-16 = 100): India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CROP.XD (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours

Why it matters — Yield gaps between India and the leaders show scope for productivity growth.

series.note: Cereal Yield: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API AG.YLD.CREL.KG (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

series.note: Cereal Yield, 2024: India ranks 12 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API AG.YLD.CREL.KG (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Cereal Production per Person
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Cereal production divided by population, derived from two official series. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 269.57 kg per person in 2024. A rising line means harvests are outpacing population.

Why it matters — Per-person output shows food self-reliance.

series.note: Cereal Production per Person: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 269.57 kg per person. Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CREL.MT, SP.POP.TOTL (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

series.note: Cereal Production per Person, 2024: India ranks 10 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CREL.MT, SP.POP.TOTL (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2025

How to read it — The line ends at 531.67 USD bn (2015 prices) in 2025. A rising line is real growth in farm sector output.

Why it matters — It shows how much farm output is expanding in real terms.

series.note: Agriculture Value Added: India's annual series, 1980 to 2025; the latest value is 531.67 USD bn (2015 prices). Source: World Bank API NV.AGR.TOTL.KD (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

Why it matters — It shows how much farm output is expanding in real terms.

series.note: Agriculture Value Added, 2025: India ranks 2 of 13 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API NV.AGR.TOTL.KD (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Land Under Cereal Production
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Area harvested for cereals. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 107.67 million hectares in 2024. A flat line while production rises means yield gains.

Why it matters — Cereal area shows land constraints on food growth.

series.note: Land Under Cereal Production: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 107.67 million hectares. Source: World Bank API AG.LND.CREL.HA (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. Higher bars show food-export dependence.

Why it matters — India's food export share indicates its role in feeding the world.

series.note: Food Exports: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API TX.VAL.FOOD.ZS.UN (FAO / WTO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.
